title: To court a mate, a male prairie chicken inflates orange air sacs on his neck

cover.alt: A brown, barred greater prairie chicken stands in green grass in evening light.

body: Each spring, from late March through April, male greater prairie chickens gather on patches of open ground called booming grounds and display there for almost two months. A displaying male raises tufts of long, dark feathers on his neck, inflates the **bare orange patches** on the sides of his neck into air sacs and snaps his tail, all to catch the eye of the females. The ritual, called booming, is the bird's most famous habit. The species name *cupido* comes from those raised feathers, which reminded naturalists of Cupid's wings.

slides.alt: A male greater prairie chicken in green grass leans forward, raises his tail and two tufts of dark feathers like horns, puffs out two round orange sacs on his neck, then turns around.
slides.caption: A male greater prairie chicken displays in Illinois in April 2010: he leans forward, raises his tail and his long neck feathers, puffs out his orange air sacs, then spins.

slides.text: Habitat loss is the greatest threat the bird has faced. Illinois once had millions of prairie chickens; in 2019, about 200 were left in the wild there.

slides.question: Where does the species name cupido come from?
slides.explanation: The long feathers the male raises during his display were thought to look like the wings of Cupid, the Roman god of love.
